name: Olga Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work in the school office at St Brendan's, a Catholic secondary school. I take the morning calls from parents whose children are off sick, keep the attendance register, type letters home and file everything in the cabinets behind my desk. At lunch I sometimes help in the chapel with the flowers. I like knowing the families, and I like that the school still does things properly.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The computer side. The attendance system has changed twice since I started, and Mrs Doyle (the school business manager) has had to show me the same screens more than once. I don't use any AI, and I don't want to. I'm getting married next summer to Piotr (my fiancé, an electrician), and I live with my parents, so I've saved a good amount.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm glad, and that people got carried away. A school runs on people who know the children, not on gadgets. I'd say that to the other office ladies over tea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel safe. St Brendan's doesn't have money for fancy systems, and the head would rather fix the roof. If a tool takes the dull typing, fine, as long as someone else sets it up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am and keep my head down. Piotr and I would keep saving for the wedding and a deposit, maybe a small house near my parents. I'd go on the school's training day if I had to, but not by choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like things are as they should be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you miss if the register went fully automatic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The phone calls. When a mother rings to say her boy has a fever, I know which boy. A machine would just tick a box. I even know his older sister, who was here before him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything already on your mind, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The wedding, mostly, and the cost of everything. But we're careful, and my parents help. I don't lose sleep over money.

say: People got **carried away**, and I'm glad it stayed small.
A school runs on people who know the **children**, not gadgets.
think: St Brendan's has **no money** for fancy systems, so I feel safe.
A tool can take the **dull typing** if someone else sets it up.
do: Carry on as I am and **keep my head down**.
Keep saving with Piotr for the **wedding and a deposit**.
Attend the school **training day** only if required.
feel: **Calm**, like things are as they **should be**.
S0.quote: When a mother rings to say her boy has a fever, I know which boy. A machine would just tick a box.
fieldNote: Her sense of worth is **knowing families**, not the systems.
Money pressure is the **wedding**, eased by her parents.
She would accept AI only if **someone else** sets it up.

steps.text: Keep taking parents' sick calls and doing the register by hand
Keep saving with Piotr for the wedding and a deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's sad, and that we're losing the human side of things. But I wouldn't say the government should fix it with handouts. People should work, and firms should train their own staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job is mostly the kind of thing it would do. Letters, the register, answering the same parent questions. I'm the newest and the slowest on the computer at St Brendan's school, so I'd be the one they'd let go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and see what the school actually did, because schools are slow. If they cut the office, I'd ask Father Michael about work at the parish office, or as a teaching assistant. Piotr and I might bring the wedding forward, to be settled before anything changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried. And a bit hurt, as if the world doesn't want what I'm good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why bring the wedding forward?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd want to be married and in our own home before things get hard. Family is what holds you up. My mother always says that, and she's right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you consider learning the new tools to stay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they made me, I'd try. But I'd be slow and I'd hate it. I'd rather do work with people, like helping the children.

say: We're losing the **human side** of things, and that's sad.
Firms should **train** their own staff, not rely on **handouts**.
think: Letters, the register and parent questions are what AI **would do**.
As the **newest and slowest**, I'd be the one let go.
do: **Wait and see** what the school does.
Ask Father Michael about **parish office** or teaching assistant work.
feel: **Worried**, and **hurt** that my strengths aren't wanted.
S1.quote: I'm the newest and the slowest on the computer at St Brendan's school, so I'd be the one they'd let go.
fieldNote: Her traditional view: **work and training**, not handouts.
Faith and family shape her plan: **parish**, wedding, parents.
She'd rather move to **people work** than learn the tools.

steps.text: Wait to see whether St Brendan's actually cuts the office

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's frightening and people need to hold on to their families and their faith. I'd say firms that rush this are being greedy. I wouldn't ask the government for money, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, my office job at St Brendan's (the school where she works) is finished by 2028. Piotr (her fiancé, an electrician) would have until about 2031. His work is hands-on, so it lasts longer. After that, I don't know what either of us would do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd marry Piotr as soon as we could and we'd stay with my parents to save. I'd look for work in the school as a teaching assistant, being with the children rather than at a screen. And I'd pray, honestly, and lean on the parish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. I'd lie awake thinking about having children in that world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would it change your plans for children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I always wanted children young, and I think I'd still want them. Maybe even sooner, while Piotr still has work. My mother would help, she's said so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said firms that rush are greedy. Who else is to blame?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People who chase every new thing without thinking. Not just bosses, all of us, buying the gadgets. I'm not one for blaming the government for everything.

say: Hold on to your **family and faith**.
Firms that **rush** this are being **greedy**, but I wouldn't ask for government money.
think: Piotr's **electrician** work lasts until about **2031**, then I don't know.
do: Marry Piotr **as soon as possible** and live with my parents to save.
Look for **teaching assistant** work with the children.
Lean on the **parish** and my family.
feel: **Scared**, lying awake about having **children** in that world.
S2.quote: My office job at St Brendan's (the school where she works) is finished by 2028. Piotr (her fiancé, an electrician) would have until about 2031.
fieldNote: She tracks the **three-year gap** between her desk job and her fiancé's trade.
Her response is **family**: marry sooner, children sooner, live with parents.
She spreads blame to **everyone** chasing gadgets, not just bosses.

steps.text: Marry Piotr this year and move in with her parents
Apply for teaching assistant work at St Brendan's
Lean on her parents and the parish for support

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to prepare, so families should prepare. Save, stay close, learn something useful with your hands. Same as my grandparents would have said.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd have until about 32. Schools are slow, so I might last until then. I'd probably keep hoping it wouldn't happen, which I know isn't sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd marry next summer as planned and buy a small house near my parents, with a mortgage Piotr could cover alone. I'd ask the school about training as a teaching assistant over the next couple of years. I wouldn't touch the AI stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I could still sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes, compared with the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We wouldn't rush the wedding. With five years, we'd have time to buy a house and have a baby with both of us still earning. That makes a big difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep hoping it wouldn't happen. What would make you act?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mrs Doyle (the school business manager) telling me straight that the office was going. I'd believe her. Until then, I'd keep doing my job.

say: There's time to prepare, so **families** should prepare.
Save, stay close and learn something useful **with your hands**.
think: Schools are slow, so I might last until about **32**.
I'd keep **hoping it wouldn't happen**, which isn't sensible.
do: Buy a **small house** near my parents that Piotr could cover alone.
Train as a **teaching assistant** over the next couple of years.
S3.quote: With five years, we'd have time to buy a house and have a baby with both of us still earning.
fieldNote: Five years keeps her **wedding plan** intact.
She admits she'd **hope** rather than plan.
She'd act only when her **manager** confirms it.
Even with five years, she would **refuse AI tools** and aim for work with children.

steps.text: Train as a teaching assistant at St Brendan's
Wait for Mrs Doyle to confirm office cuts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is long enough for anyone who's willing to work. Raise your family, learn a trade, and don't wait for someone to save you. That's what I'd say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel all right. I'd be 37, married, maybe with two children, and the school office would still be there for a good while. I'd worry more about Piotr later on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd follow our plans: wedding, house, children. I'd stay at St Brendan's and maybe move into the classroom as an assistant after a few years. Piotr might take on an apprentice, because he says that's how trades should be passed on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A small worry at the back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the small worry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd be home with small children when the office goes, and have nothing to go back to. My mother went back to the bakery after having children. There might not be a bakery job for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the computer tools in ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a little, if the school trained me properly. But I'd never be the one who loves it. I'm better with people.

Raise your family, **learn a trade**, and don't wait to be saved.
think: At 37, married with children, the **school office** would still be there a while.
I'd worry more about **Piotr** later on.
do: Move into the **classroom** as an assistant after a few years.
feel: Mostly **calm**, with a **small worry** at the back.
S4.quote: My mother went back to the bakery after having children. There might not be a bakery job for me.
fieldNote: A decade fits her **family timeline** neatly.
Her hidden worry is having **nothing to return to** after children.
She values **apprenticeships** and passing on trades.

steps.text: Marry, buy a house and start a family on schedule
Move into a classroom assistant role after a few years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028. My job and then Piotr's, while we're just starting out. What would help is employers keeping people on and training them for the jobs that are left, and the church and families looking after each other.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. For me it would matter a lot, more than any app. People would need somewhere to go that isn't a screen.

headlineQuote: A school runs on people who know the children, not on gadgets.
portrait: Olga is a **27-year-old** junior in the office at St Brendan's, a Catholic secondary school.
She lives with her parents, has **strong savings**, and is marrying Piotr, an electrician, next summer.
She never uses AI and values **knowing families** over systems.
Her answer to each scenario runs through **family and faith**: marry sooner, lean on the parish.
She wants **work and training** from employers, not handouts from government.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** AGI picture, losing her job and then Piotr's while **just starting out**.
whatWouldHelp: Employers **keeping people on** and training them for remaining jobs.
Church and **families** looking after each other.
